title: What the Midterms Taught Us About the State of America’s Democracy
author: Chika O Okafor
body:
The recent “Blue Wave” was Democrats’ best election night in years. But Memphis, a majority-Black city whose own congressional seat Democrats had held for more than four decades, will be represented in Congress entirely by Republicans.

The day after the midterms, Justin Pearson, the Democratic candidate for Tennessee’s newly drawn Ninth District House seat, may have conceded his race, but he refused to concede to the redistricting. These “rigged maps”—as he called them—broke apart his voter base and were enabled by a recent Supreme Court decision that dramatically narrowed key protections of the Voting Rights Act.

Louisiana v. Callais—a case the Supreme Court decided in April—made it far easier for states to redraw district lines for political reasons, even if doing so undermined minorities’ political opportunity. About 85% of voters in Memphis’ Ninth District’s Shelby County portion supported Pearson, and Kamala Harris won the district by 44 points in 2024. But now, their elected representative to Congress will be Republican.

It is clear to legal experts like myself that redistricting harmed the political opportunity of minorities in Memphis. Before Callais, the Voting Rights Act protected against such redistricting efforts. But that is no longer the case.

This is because the Supreme Court has enshrined a new colorblind standard in the Voting Rights Act that extends its 2023 decision ending race-based college admissions. This standard makes it nearly impossible for the Voting Rights Act to operate as Congress intended. Now, it is not enough to show racial harm. Plaintiffs must provide evidence supporting a “strong inference” that maps were drawn through intentional racial discrimination not explainable by politics. They also cannot use race themselves in proposing alternative maps—with such maps still needing to satisfy the state’s political objectives.

The thinking that this new colorblind standard promotes fairness is flawed. My economics research—published in The Journal of Law and Economics—explains why. I originated the concept of social network discrimination, demonstrating mathematically that minorities receive fewer economic and social opportunities systematically, all else being equal, simply because their social group is smaller. Driven by the tendency for people to form relationships with others like themselves, this disadvantage compounds across the political process, suggesting social network discrimination also applies to redistricting and can limit political opportunity. As these networks often form along racial lines, partisan divides can partly be a consequence of race.

The Supreme Court instead treats politics as a race-neutral explanation for why a map harms minority voters. Thus, according to Callais’s logic, the more race shapes partisan patterns, the stronger the legal defense states have for gerrymandering that harms racial minorities: partisanship. That happened in Memphis. A federal court refused to block the redrawn map because “political motivations readily explain the map’s dilutive effects.”

Granted, we all just witnessed a Blue Wave. So maybe this Callais decision does not matter so much? No, the decision still matters today and will matter much more in future elections. For one, a preliminary analysis from The New York Times estimates the new maps yielded four to seven additional Republican House seats on net—with gerrymandering overall potentially preventing a veto-proof Democratic supermajority. Plus, the decision will impact who decides to even run for office in the first place. Though Democratic Congressman Shomari Figures from Alabama still decided to run after redistricting (and won 54% to 46%), Louisiana Congressman Cleo Fields, a Democrat, decided not to run for reelection after his district was redrawn. Which candidates have viable paths to victory will very likely change. And so will who remains on the ballot, with some candidates opting instead for different offices, or entirely different careers.

In my view, the Blue Wave says much less about the long-term impact of Callais on election outcomes and political opportunity, and much more about both shorter-term disapproval of the current administration and voter turnout. With significantly higher prices on items like gasoline, many Americans wanted change. This imperative—along with a likely surge in Black voter turnout across the South, at least in part in reaction to the Callais decision—helped feed the Blue Wave. But a question remains: will such a surge persist through the next presidency—as outrage over the Callais decision fades from the national conversation? This Blue Wave is likely the exception, not the rule.

In fact, this midterm season witnessed truly historic victories for Democrats and minorities. Texas elected its first Latina governor. Georgia elected its first Black governor—and the nation’s first Black female one. Illinois elected its second Black female U.S. senator. Michigan—and the nation—elected its first Muslim U.S. senator. Mississippi elected its first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. Yet all these historic milestones came from statewide wins in a wave year. Statewide races are also ones neither immediately nor directly impacted by redistricting—and thus by Callais. The new legal standard established by this decision will last long after 2026—long after this Blue Wave crests. Key Voting Rights Act protections still remain difficult to enforce. Ruthless political gerrymandering still remains largely unrestrained—with a federal court in Louisiana now weighing a challenge to the sole remaining majority-Black district there. Equal political opportunity for minorities still remains endangered.

So, despite the “Blue Wave,” American democracy still remains in the red. And it will remain that way unless Congress or the Supreme Court acts—regardless of the outcome in this singular election, or even which party wins the next one.
